clinicalPearls: Two genetically distinct forms: type I from biallelic D2HGDH mutations (autosomal recessive) and type II from a de novo gain-of-function IDH2 mutation (dominant); type II tends to be more severe.
Typical presentation is in infancy with developmental delay, hypotonia, epilepsy or epileptic encephalopathy, and, especially in type II, cardiomyopathy.
The same neomorphic IDH2 mutations drive gliomas and acute myeloid leukaemia as somatic events; here they occur in the germline/de novo and D-2-hydroxyglutarate behaves as an oncometabolite.
Urine organic acid analysis shows raised 2-hydroxyglutarate, but chiral (enantiomer) separation is essential to distinguish the D form from the L form and the combined D,L form.
Brain MRI may show subependymal pseudocysts, enlarged ventricles and delayed cerebral maturation with abnormal gyration and myelination.
Diagnosis is confirmed by quantifying the D-enantiomer in body fluids and by sequencing D2HGDH and IDH2; plasma and cerebrospinal fluid can also be tested.
Management is largely supportive with seizure control and cardiac surveillance; riboflavin and other measures have been tried without robust proven benefit.
reference.pathophysiology: D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria results from accumulation of D-2-hydroxyglutarate in body fluids and brain. Type I is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in D2HGDH, encoding D-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase, which normally oxidises D-2-hydroxyglutarate back to 2-oxoglutarate (alpha-ketoglutarate). Type II is caused by a heterozygous de novo gain-of-function mutation in IDH2, the mitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase, typically at an arginine residue (R140), conferring a neomorphic activity that reduces alpha-ketoglutarate to D-2-hydroxyglutarate. The accumulated D-2-hydroxyglutarate acts as an oncometabolite, competitively inhibiting alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases including histone and DNA demethylases and prolyl hydroxylases, thereby disturbing epigenetic regulation, hypoxia signalling and cellular metabolism, which underlies the neurological and cardiac phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Combined D,L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (SLC25A1 / mitochondrial citrate carrier deficiency)
Glutaric aciduria type I and other organic acidurias
Other causes of neonatal or infantile epileptic encephalopathy
Metabolic cardiomyopathies (e.g. Barth syndrome, fatty acid oxidation defects)
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acid analysis with chiral separation of 2-hydroxyglutarate enantiomers
Molecular testing of D2HGDH and IDH2
Echocardiography and ECG for cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia
Enzyme activity or functional assays where available
redFlags: New or worsening cardiomyopathy or signs of heart failure
Status epilepticus or medically refractory seizures
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable: type I ranges from mild to severe, whereas type II is generally more severe with early cardiomyopathy and higher mortality. No curative therapy exists, and prognosis is determined mainly by the degree of neurological and cardiac involvement.
pitfalls: Failing to perform chiral separation, so D- and L-enantiomers are not distinguished.
Assuming autosomal recessive inheritance in all cases and missing de novo dominant IDH2 disease, which changes recurrence-risk counselling.
Overlooking cardiomyopathy, which can be life-threatening, particularly in type II.
Attributing modest biochemical elevations to other organic acidurias without enantiomer-specific testing.
management: Coordinate care through a metabolic medicine service; no curative therapy exists, so treatment is supportive and directed at the neurological and cardiac manifestations
Control seizures and epileptic encephalopathy with antiepileptic drugs selected for the seizure type and guided by EEG
Manage cardiomyopathy, particularly in the more severe type II, with standard heart-failure pharmacotherapy alongside surveillance echocardiography and ECG for arrhythmia
Provide developmental support with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and feeding or nutritional input for hypotonia and delay
Offer genetic counselling that distinguishes autosomal recessive type I (biallelic D2HGDH) from the de novo dominant IDH2 gain-of-function type II, with family testing as appropriate
Escalate promptly for cardiac decompensation, arrhythmia or status epilepticus
